module_title: State Legislature - Comparative Powers, Deadlocks, and Assent
introduction: This advanced level analyzes the massive power disparity between the Assembly and the Council, the process of resolving legislative deadlocks (and the absence of joint sittings), and the Governor's power to reserve bills for the President.

core_concepts.title: Ordinary Bills & The Council's Limitations
core_concepts.description: If an ordinary bill originates in the Assembly, the Council can delay it for a maximum of 3 months the first time. If the Assembly passes it again, the Council can delay it for only 1 more month. (Total maximum delay = 4 months). The Council can delay, but CANNOT kill an ordinary bill.

core_concepts.title: No Provision for Joint Sittings
core_concepts.description: Unlike the Parliament, where the President can summon a Joint Sitting (Article 108) to resolve a deadlock, there is NO provision for a joint sitting in a state legislature. The will of the Legislative Assembly ultimately prevails.

core_concepts.title: Money Bills
core_concepts.description: Similar to the Parliament, a Money Bill can only be introduced in the Legislative Assembly. The Legislative Council has extremely restricted powers and can only delay a Money Bill for a maximum of 14 days.

core_concepts.title: Reservation of Bills (Articles 200 & 201)
core_concepts.description: Under Article 200, the Governor can reserve a bill for the President's consideration. If the President returns it for reconsideration and the state legislature passes it again, the President is STILL NOT bound to give assent (unlike Central bills, where the President must give assent upon repassage).

important_entities.name: Legislative Assembly
important_entities.description: Because there are no joint sittings and the Council's delaying power is strictly capped at 4 months, the Legislative Assembly is the undisputed and absolute center of legislative power in a state.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: A major conceptual trap: Students often equate their powers. The Rajya Sabha can delay an ordinary bill for 6 months, and its disagreement leads to a Joint Sitting. The Legislative Council can only delay for 4 months, and its disagreement is overridden by the Assembly. The Council is much weaker.
While the Governor has discretion to reserve bills for the President, it is CONSTITUTIONALLY MANDATORY to reserve any bill that endangers the position or powers of the State High Court.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: 3 months during the first instance + 1 month during the second instance = 4 months total maximum delay for an ordinary bill.

exam_strategy_tips: In UPSC Assertion-Reasoning questions, thoroughly understand the implications of the 'absence of a joint sitting' and how it renders the Legislative Council subservient to the Assembly.
Pay close attention to questions testing the difference between the President's veto power over Central bills versus State bills (Article 201).
